name: Crucible Heart

detectability.signature: A slow spiral of blue-white discharge with a clean rotational signature; sensors read it as a lighthouse that sweeps in three dimensions at once.

proximity: Power systems run hot and batteries charge whether you want them to or not
Fine manipulation of equipment becomes difficult; tools drift on induced currents
contact: Unshielded craft take progressive electrical damage to guidance systems
Crew receive painful but rarely lethal shocks through suit contact points
prolonged_exposure: Cumulative damage to solid-state electronics; most ships exit with something permanently dimmer
Documented cases of persistent static charge in crew hair and temper for weeks afterward

age: indeterminate; observed for at least 400 years

behavior.cycle: 7-hour rotation, brightening at each pole passage

phenomena: The vortex's spiral arms are visible from millions of kilometers as a faint blue pinwheel
Ships passing nearby report their radios playing fragments of other ships' traffic, cleanly separated by channel
Ice crystals drawn into the volume emerge polished into near-perfect spheres
hazards: Electrical surge damage to unshielded systems during pole-passage peaks
Induced currents strong enough to injure crew in contact with hull extremities
opportunities: A free, endless charge point: ships routinely top off capacitors at the boundary with proper grounding discipline
The vortex's rotation provides a fixed timing reference used to synchronize the sector's civilian navigation network
known_incidents: The first survey ship to probe the interior lost main power and drifted for two days before being towed out; her captain's report coined the standing rule: 'charge, don't touch.'
During the border disputes a century ago, a militia flotilla hid inside the vortex's volume; the pursuing squadron's electronics failed in sequence, and the flotilla walked out untouched.
description: Crucible Heart is a pinwheel of contained lightning: a spherical volume a fifth of an astronomical unit across where ionized gas spirals around an invisible axis, glowing blue-white and sweeping its brightness past any observer every seven hours. It looks manufactured. No natural model quite produces it, and no one has found wreckage, structure, or purpose at its center.

The vortex is energetic but honest. Its seven-hour rhythm never falters for long, its boundary is sharp, and its effects scale cleanly with proximity: warmth and drift at the edge, pain and damage at the core. Ships that respect the geometry come away charged; ships that blunder in come away limping. Both outcomes are documented across four centuries of records.

Found by a trade tender four hundred years ago and named for the forge it resembled, the Heart has been everything from a hazard to a hideout to a power station. The militia incident made it legend; the navigation contract made it infrastructure. Every clock in the sector is quietly set by its sweep, which means the anomaly nobody can explain is also the one nobody can do without.

Research continues into its origin, with the leading candidates being a collapsed megastructure, a fossil of some ancient engine, and a natural formation everyone is too embarrassed to keep failing to model. Meanwhile the harvest crews moor at the boundary each cycle, ground their lines, and top off. The Heart asks only that you not touch.
